item.content:encoded: In May 2019, Kenyum Bagra, a Ph.D. student from Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Roorkee, was collecting river water and sediment samples at multiple locations in Uttarakhand, along Bindal Rao and Rispana, two heavily polluted sub-tributaries of the Ganga river, flowing through Dehradun’s densely populated settlements. While Rispana is a perennial stream, she noted that Bindal, a seasonal river, was dry at upstream locations, as expected at this time before the arrival of the monsoon (between June and September) except near the settlements where there was a slim flow. This flow was the city’s wastewater that drains into the riverbed throughout the year. Running in parallel, Rispana and Bindal respectively carry almost 10 million litres per day (MLD) and about 18 MLD of municipal wastewater, before joining downstream to form the Suswa river, a polluted river stretch listed under the Namami Gange river restoration programme. Bagra also noticed that both rivers were being used to dump solid waste. “During my work, I saw solid waste dumped directly into these rivers, as well as dead animals, while children were playing and bathing just downstream,” says Bagra, now an Assistant Professor at IIT-Varanasi. Based on seasonal (pre-monsoon, monsoon and post-monsoon) and multilocational samplings in 2019, Bagra’s mentor Gargi Singh, Associate Professor, IIT-Roorkee, recently reported that throughout the sampling stretches, these rivers showed widespread faecal and anthropogenic pollution. Monsoon rainfall was also associated with a surge in antibiotic resistance genes (ARG) in both of these rivers. item.content:encoded: In the villages of the Western Ghats, some of the oldest and tallest trees do not grow inside a national park. They grow in sacred groves, small patches of old, mostly untouched forest that local communities have protected for generations, because they believe the trees belong to their deities and ancestors. A new study published in the journal PLOS One found that young trees regenerate far more successfully in these groves. Seeds dropped by fruit-eating birds are much likelier to survive and grow there than in surrounding farms and villages. India has more than 100,000 sacred groves, which are recognised as essential to community-based conservation. The Western Ghats is a mountain range that runs about 1,600 kilometres down India’s west coast, across six states. The study began there by chance. A team from the Applied Environmental Research Foundation (AERF), which runs a giant-tree programme, had signed up a man in Vanzole village with a huge Terminalia bellirica (beheda) tree in his yard. Visiting, they saw giant trees all over the village. “It sparked a series of questions,” study co-author Kevin Matteson, associate director of Project Dragonfly at Miami University in the U.S. state of Ohio, told Mongabay in an email. How many giant trees were hiding in plain sight, and were birds like hornbills really using trees in such busy places? To find out, the team walked the whole village with two local experts, Namdev and Anant Shivgan, who mapped the land, identified the trees and led the team to…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.content:encoded: Geeta Devi is a resident of Gandhi Tola in Manihari, Katihar district, Bihar, one of the 15 districts worst hit by this year’s floods. Waist-deep water fills her three-room mud house, which is still standing. But she isn’t sure how long it will hold. She has kept her valuable belongings in an elevated place. Almost every day, the 35-year-old farmer braves the water to go from her makeshift shelter to her house check how much the water has risen and whether her things are safe. Geeta’s husband is in Delhi where he works as a daily-wage labourer, leaving her in charge of the flooded household, agricultural field, livestock and her four children. Scale of the losses Bihar is facing severe flooding, with the Ganga and several other rivers flowing above the danger mark. The Kosi is flowing above the danger mark at Baltara and Kursela, while the Budhi Gandak is above the mark at Khagaria. The Ganga is above the danger mark at Digha, Gandhi Ghat, Hathidah, Bhagalpur, Kahalgaon and Munger. The Punpun is above the mark at Paliganj, while the Bagmati and Ghaghra are above the danger mark at Benibad and Darauli. The floods have affected 15 districts of Bihar, with almost 50 lakh (5 million) people affected across 88 blocks and 575 gram panchayats, according to the state government’s press release dated September 14, 2026. item.content:encoded: This is Part 2 of a series on exotic pet trade. The series looks at the health impacts, legal challenges and the ecological consequences of keeping exotic wild animals as pets. Part 1 elaborates on how the trade enables zoonoses or zoonotic disease spillovers. Recently, pictures and videos of five orangutan babies in a forest in Odisha, thousands of miles from their real home, were plastered across many screens. As authorities investigate the antecedents of the critically endangered animals and discuss their future, one thing is becoming increasingly clear: international wildlife trafficking is widening its reach, and India is emerging as a destination. Keeping exotic animals and birds as pets, is not new in India. Non-native parrots have long dominated the scene. But keeping them legally involves navigating a complex set of legal procedures. The repertoire of species illegally reaching Indian shores, however, has expanded significantly in recent years. Primates are the new parrots. Gibbons, lemurs, marmosets and macaques, once difficult to find outside their native ranges, are increasingly turning up in seizures linked to the illegal pet trade. Primates are a group of mammals that includes humans, apes, monkeys, lemurs and lorises, generally characterised by grasping hands and feet, forward-facing eyes and relatively large brains. The seizure of an orangutan from an apartment bathroom in Mumbai in 2024, a Tamil actor’s pet Lar gibbon, and the controversy over two lemurs at Vantara highlight the emerging trade. He was caught unaware: He says he wasn’t aware that the forest department was trying to capture a tiger roaming through the areas. Before he realised […]
item.content:encoded: Forty-five-year-old Mahadeva Gowda was tending to his cotton farm in the village of Badagalapura in the southern Indian state of Karnataka when a tiger lunged at him from behind. He was caught unaware: He says he wasn’t aware that the forest department was trying to capture a tiger roaming through the areas. Before he realised what was happening, the tiger swiped at his face, severely injuring his eyes and part of his face. After multiple reconstructive surgeries, Gowda has been left to live the rest of his life blinded, without eyes, his mouth only able to open partially, and his speech slurred. His wife, Indrani, says survival is extremely difficult for the family; Gowda was the household’s breadwinner, and now, he can’t work. He’s now become fully dependent on his wife for even his most basic needs. The incident occurred in mid-October 2025. Two weeks later, another farmer, 55-year-old Rajashekarappa, was grazing his cattle in a field when he encountered a tiger. It was fatal. Badagalapura and other villages that regularly report tiger encounters sit on the edge of the forest, placing them within what the forest department considers a “tiger landscape.” “Tigers have been present in this landscape for centuries and they constantly move here,” says S. Prabhakaran, who served as conservator of forests and oversaw operations at Karnataka’s Bandipur Tiger Reserve until earlier this year. The 1,456-square-kilometre park is home to between 154 and 175 tigers, according to a 2024 estimate by India’s National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA).…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Reviving Himachal’s traditional Kath-Kuni homes to beat the heat
item.dc:creator: Rachna Verma
item.author: Kartik Chandramouli
item.topic-tags: Climate Change Adaptation, Himalayas, and Sustainability
item.description: As Himachal Pradesh warms, people are reconsidering traditional Kath-Kuni homes for more than their cultural and architectural value. For generations, people in parts of the state built houses by interlocking layers of locally sourced timber and stone. The thick walls, wooden bands and locally adapted construction helped homes withstand the region’s earthquakes and harsh winters. […]
item.content:encoded: As Himachal Pradesh warms, people are reconsidering traditional Kath-Kuni homes for more than their cultural and architectural value. For generations, people in parts of the state built houses by interlocking layers of locally sourced timber and stone. The thick walls, wooden bands and locally adapted construction helped homes withstand the region’s earthquakes and harsh winters. Today, some families also find that these houses offer a different kind of comfort during increasingly warming summers. “We decided that we wanted a wooden house because it naturally maintains the temperature. It stays cool in summer and warm in winter,” says Asha Thakur, who is rebuilding her home in Kullu using the Kath-Kuni tradition. Her family waited almost two years for master mason Bhagat Ram, who has spent around 25 years learning and practising the craft. He describes the experience of being inside these houses simply: “These houses become pleasantly cool inside. It’s just like sitting under the shade of a tree on a hot day.” “It is a passive climate regulation system,” says Professor Thanshwimong Chowdhury of IIT-Mandi, who is studying materials and heat transmissibility in this traditional architectural style. As the Himalaya warms, can an old way of building become part of the response to a changing climate? This film was produced under Mongabay-India and ALT EFF’s Video Reporting Opportunity programme. Watch more videos from this series: How a village in Bastar in stopping forest fires How Maldharis find freshwater in one of India’s hottest landscapes  This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.description: On August 31, the Permanent Court of Arbitration — an intergovernmental body headquartered in The Hague — passed an order that said India could not unilaterally retreat from or cast aside the Indus Waters Treaty, a 66-year-old pact governing water sharing between India and Pakistan. India rejected the court’s decision shortly after, prolonging the deadlock […]
item.content:encoded: On August 31, the Permanent Court of Arbitration — an intergovernmental body headquartered in The Hague — passed an order that said India could not unilaterally retreat from or cast aside the Indus Waters Treaty, a 66-year-old pact governing water sharing between India and Pakistan. India rejected the court’s decision shortly after, prolonging the deadlock between both countries and throwing the Treaty’s future into a state of flux. The PCA’s order was issued more than a year after India placed the agreement in “abeyance” following attacks by militants that India said were linked to Pakistan-based groups. “India’s position on the Indus Waters Treaty is consistent. The IWT stands in abeyance in response to Pakistan’s continued sponsorship of cross-border terrorism. Pakistan must credibly and irrevocably abjure its support for cross-border terrorism,” Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal told the press in July. The PCA said it contemplated the meaning of India’s decision, since the word “abeyance” finds no recognition in the Treaty. It concluded that none of the grounds publicly cited by India “could justify suspension or termination of the Treaty,” and that it “remains fully in force, and India must observe its obligations.” Though famously having remained intact through three wars, the ongoing suspension has reinforced the need to modernise the agreement, experts say, so it can account for geopolitical differences, climate impacts, and changing water consumption habits. “If rights under an agreement cannot be exercised within a period of time without uncertainty, then it means that process isn’t…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.description: In the high-altitude landscapes of Himachal Pradesh, conservation efforts have long revolved around the charismatic snow leopard (Panthera uncia). But a new study suggests this focus may be leaving a host of other ecologically vital species outside the conservation umbrella. The study, led by scientists from the Nature Conservation Foundation and partner institutions, mapped the […]
item.content:encoded: In the high-altitude landscapes of Himachal Pradesh, conservation efforts have long revolved around the charismatic snow leopard (Panthera uncia). But a new study suggests this focus may be leaving a host of other ecologically vital species outside the conservation umbrella. The study, led by scientists from the Nature Conservation Foundation and partner institutions, mapped the distribution of Galliformes — a group of heavy-bodied, ground-dwelling birds that includes pheasants and partridges — across 26,000 square kilometres. It found that only 12.5% of areas with high Galliformes species richness and 8.8% of areas with high concentrations of endemic species fall within existing protected areas (PA), designated zones for conservation of wildlife and habitats. The findings indicate that important bird habitats lie outside the designated protected areas. They point to the need for conservation planning that considers multiple species and the landscapes they share, rather than focusing mainly on flagship species such as the snow leopard. Snow leopard cameras reveal bird conservation gap The study, however, did not begin with birds at all. It grew out of a snow leopard survey conducted between 2016 and 2019. “We deployed close to 300 camera traps to estimate snow leopard populations,” said Kulbhushansingh Suryawanshi, a scientist with the Nature Conservation Foundation, and senior author of the paper. “We completed that work and published those results. That is when we realised that while studying these charismatic species, our camera traps had detected many other animals.” Suryawanshi and his team revisited the data to identify species that warranted…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.content:encoded: The banks of the Barana river, where those affected by the Ken-Betwa project led the Panchtatva Satyagraha in July, now lie quiet. Although water levels have risen to cover much of the protest site, traces of the chita (pyre) and phansi (noose) used for demonstrations are still visible. The din of machinery can constantly be heard from beneath the nearby bridge. A large number of slippers lie scattered near the bridge, left behind during police interventions on July 19. Bhagwati Saur, 60, who lives 30 km away in Mainari village in Chhatarpur district in Madhya Pradesh, arrived on July 4 at the protest site in Kupi village and returned home after the police cleared the site. She lives with her husband and six children in a five-room house. The family owns approximately five acres of agricultural land, where they grow mango, mahua and guava trees. She says that despite being affected by the project, she has, so far, received neither compensation for the house and land nor any related notice. “We pleaded for fair compensation, taking our appeal from Chhatarpur to Bhopal. When we were not heard, we had to raise our voices through the protest,” says Bhagwati. She is not the only one. In the affected villages, some families have been written off the compensation list, while others are awaiting payment. Many families are questioning the compensation rates and survey process. The April and July protests prompted the administration to order a reassessment of the families that had been left…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: The crane that loves a duet
item.dc:creator: Team Mongabay-India
item.author: Aditi Tandon
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Birds, Conservation, Ecology, Endangered species, Environment, and Wildlife
item.description: The female sarus crane typically initiates the duet, which has a three-part structure: an introduction, trill and main segment.
item.content:encoded: Species File: Exploring India’s biodiversity, one species at a time. A new study of sarus cranes across the agricultural landscapes of Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Gujarat found that the birds follow a three-part structure in their duets, loud, coordinated calls produced by mating pairs. The female typically initiates the duet, which has an introduction, trill and main segment. While the acoustic details vary between populations and pairs, the researchers found no distinct regional “dialects”. The sarus crane (Antigone antigone) is the world’s tallest flying bird, standing up to 1.8 meters with a wingspan of 2.4 meters. The birds are recognisable through their grey bodies with a bright red neck and head. Unlike songbirds, sarus cranes have a more primitive vocal system called the pharynx and a limited number of vocalisations. While males and females are visually difficult to distinguish, researchers have found a way to tell them apart through the notes in their calls. The state bird of Uttar Pradesh, sarus cranes are mostly found in wetlands, grasslands and agricultural landscape. Its numbers are rising particularly in Uttar Pradesh’s Rohilkhand region. A total of 1,942 sarus cranes have been recorded in the region and forest department officials say the increase reflects ongoing conservation efforts, especially in wetlands and marshy areas, and is a boost for ecological balance. The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List of Species categorises the sarus crane as vulnerable, which means it faces a high risk of extinction in the wild. By evening, an intense itch had developed around her eyelids and lips. Her mother had similar allergic reactions on her hands. Several doctors’ consultations and treatments followed. Doctors […]
item.content:encoded: On a June morning in 2025, 24-year-old Niharika Deka of Kaliabor in Nagaon district, Assam, took the family’s cattle out to graze, filling in for her mother. By evening, an intense itch had developed around her eyelids and lips. Her mother had similar allergic reactions on her hands. Several doctors’ consultations and treatments followed. Doctors initially suspected a cosmetic trigger. “The symptoms eased with medication, but the itch would flare up the moment I stepped into the fields or sometimes even outside the house. We kept shuttling between doctors,” Deka said. The picture became clearer when other villagers and students began reporting similar rashes and allergic episodes on exposed skin. Suspicion narrowed to a small, white-flowering wild plant that had recently begun proliferating across the locality. When its conspicuous flowering subsided after August, the allergies eased too. When the flowers returned in the summer of 2026, so did the itching. Deka said the repeated flare-ups have left dark patches around her eyelids and mouth, with similar discolouration on her mother’s hands. “It looks awful, and we don’t know if it’ll fade. I’m of marriageable age, and my parents are worried,” she said. About 150 km away, in Raja Mayong in Morigaon district, farmer Mahesh Nath is grappling with the same weed on his one-acre plot, where he grows vegetables and grains for a living. “It outpaces everything else,” he said. item.content:encoded: Amid increasing climate impacts and a fractured geopolitical order, the BRICS Summit in India underlined the importance of climate resilience in the New Delhi Declaration, along with energy security as a crucial foundation for social and economic development, national security and the welfare of all nations. The New Delhi Declaration, a consensus document adopted on September 12 by countries in the BRICS bloc, underlined the role of fossil fuels in the world’s energy mix, particularly for emerging markets and developing economies. The expanded BRICS grouping comprises 21 countries, including 11 members and 10 partner countries. India assumed the BRICS Chairship in January, and the 18th BRICS Leaders’ Summit took place on September 12 and 13 in New Delhi. The declaration recognises the importance of the energy transition and reducing greenhouse gas emissions, but also emphasises the principles of technological neutrality and common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities (CBDR-RC). The declaration also outlines areas for practical cooperation, including carbon markets, climate research and community-based adaptation. It calls for greater collaboration on smart grids, energy storage, hydrogen, critical minerals and efforts to decarbonise transport. Recognising the disproportionate burden climate change imposes across countries, the declaration expresses resolve to remain united in pursuit of the purpose, principles and objectives of the UNFCCC and its Paris Agreement. It also calls on all countries to uphold their existing commitments and scale up their efforts to combat climate change. item.description: More than 1,386 people have died and over 5,130 more missing, as of September 12, following the August 26 floods in Nepal. In the wreckage along the Bhote Koshi river lie two unresolved questions: Is climate change linked to the disaster? And, can a nascent global fund, built to help vulnerable countries in such crises, […]
item.content:encoded: More than 1,386 people have died and over 5,130 more missing, as of September 12, following the August 26 floods in Nepal. In the wreckage along the Bhote Koshi river lie two unresolved questions: Is climate change linked to the disaster? And, can a nascent global fund, built to help vulnerable countries in such crises, actually deliver? Soon after the floods, the Government of Nepal wrote a letter to the Board of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD), a financial mechanism of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) established in 2022 to help vulnerable countries cope with climate disasters. In the letter signed by the country’s Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle and Minister for Agriculture, Forest and Environment Gita Chaudhary, Nepal requested the board to take a special decision to respond rapidly, directly and effectively. Signed on August 31, the letter emphasised that a prompt response would “demonstrate that the Fund can translate international solidarity into timely support for vulnerable countries and communities when it is most urgently needed.” Nepal contributes roughly 0.027% of global greenhouse gas emissions. The mountainous country is in the ‘least developed country’ category designated by the UN and is a highly climate-vulnerable country that “continues to bear disproportionate and escalating climate impacts,” the letter states. It argues that the Bhote Koshi disaster demonstrates how extreme events in the cryosphere can rapidly cascade and compound from high mountains to densely populated downstream areas, affecting water, food, energy, health, infrastructure and ecosystems. item.content:encoded: An endemic plant species Rungia mastersii was rediscovered in Assam, 180 years after its first discovery. The plant was not seen anywhere during this period. Kangkan Kumar Das, a doctoral researcher, and professor Debjyoti Bhattacharyya from the Department of Life Science and Bioinformatics at Assam University, Silchar, identified the species from Jatinga Hills in the Dima Hasao district of Assam. In 1845, British botanist J.W. Masters first discovered the plant from an unidentified location along Assam’s Sundar river and the plant was named after Masters. Speaking to Mongabay-India, Das said, “I was pursuing my doctoral research on the Acanthaceae family of plants and was travelling through Assam for my research. In Jatinga hills in Dima Hasao, I found this plant Rungia mastersii which is also a member of the family Acanthaceae. After I discovered this plant, I consulted with the renowned Chinese botanist Prof. Yunfei Deng from South China Botanical Garden who confirmed it.” He informed that for almost two centuries, there was no trace of this plant anywhere in the world. “Only one herbarium sheet has been kept at Central National Herbarium (CNH), Howrah,” he said. The endemic plant species Rungia mastersii was rediscovered in Assam after 180 years in Jatinga Hills, Dima Hasao district. Image by Kangkan Kumar Das. At an estimated ₹1,385 crores (₹13.85 billion), the tunnel will cost about ₹622 crore (₹6.22 billion) per kilometre. The tunnel’s […]
item.content:encoded: The proposed three-lane, bidirectional tunnel road in north Bengaluru, intended to ease congestion at Hebbal Junction — a major interchange connecting the airport with the rest of the city — has run into rough weather. At an estimated ₹1,385 crores (₹13.85 billion), the tunnel will cost about ₹622 crore (₹6.22 billion) per kilometre. The tunnel’s long-term benefits in terms of easing traffic congestion are, however, unclear. A recent analysis by the Sustainable Transportation Lab of the Indian Institute of Science (IISc ) points out that the tunnel is a “highly localised improvement” that “merely shifts the congestion point”, leaving bottlenecks at its entry and exit. The detailed project report or DPR shows that by 2047, the tunnel will operate at or beyond capacity in all scenarios modelled. According to urban mobility expert Satya Arikutharam, apart from creating more chaos at these bottlenecks, the tunnel “will also worsen the local traffic, the very problem it intends to solve. Faster arrival rate at these local road intersections due to the new short  tunnel capacity means quicker accumulation of traffic, queuing pile-ups and traffic jams,” he says. Groundwater and flooding concerns A bigger concern the citizens and environmental experts are raising is about the risks it could pose to groundwater and flooding. The little over two-kilometre tunnel will run from the Hebbal flyover junction in north Bengaluru — about 30 km by road from Kempegowda International Airport — to the Veterinary College. item.content:encoded: Among the 12 bills passed during the Monsoon Session of Parliament concluded in August, the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 (MMDR Amendment Bill) has drawn the most opposition. The bill — which has far-reaching implications for Centre-State relations and the federal structure — was introduced in the Lok Sabha on August 10 and passed by a voice vote within two minutes on August 12. The statement of objects and reasons accompanying the Bill states that centre has assumed control over the regulation of mines and the development of minerals under Section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, “in view of the larger public interest.” These amendments significantly alter the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, shifting authority over mineral-bearing land from states to the Union Government. States can no longer impose any tax, cess or levy on such land, whether based on mineral quantity, prices, royalty or any other basis, other than the terms or restrictions prescribed by the Centre. States had won this right to levy taxes following a 2024 Supreme Court ruling, which also ordered them to recover outstanding dues in 12 installments starting April 1, 2025. However, states will not be required to return the amounts already collected. Opposition parties allege that mining-rich states will suffer a revenue loss following the amendment to the MMDR Act. item.content:encoded: Every summer, the forests around Tiriya village in Bastar, Chhattisgarh, face the threat of fire. But before flames can spread, the residents are already on the move. Members of Tiriya’s gram sabha patrol the forest on bicycles, looking for fresh smoke or flames. They work in shifts, maintain firelines and coordinate with the Forest Department when fires are detected. The patrols are part of a larger change in how the community manages its forests. After receiving Community Forest Resource rights in 2022-23, Tiriya’s gram sabha took responsibility for more than 3,000 hectares of forest. Villagers say this changed how they viewed and managed the forest. “Now, the villagers have reduced burning and monitor planned fires closely,” says Loknath Nag, who is part of the village’s Community Forest Resource Management Committee. For the Dhurwa community, mahua and sal are important to food, livelihoods and traditions, while forest produce such as mushrooms depends on the leaf litter that fires can destroy. The community’s efforts appear to be paying off. Recorded fires in Tiriya fell from 19 to three between 2022 and 2025, with one recorded by May 2026, according to the gram sabha and forest department. Watch Before The Fire to see how Tiriya’s community-led forest patrols work and what it takes to keep a fire from becoming a forest fire.   This film was produced under Mongabay-India and ALT EFF’s Video Reporting Opportunity programme.This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.content:encoded: Krishna AchutaRao, the renowned climate scientist and a professor at IIT Delhi’s Centre for Atmospheric Sciences (CAS), died on September 4, aged 62. AchutaRao’s research helped strengthen the science of climate attribution, distinguishing climate change related events from ordinary ones. His sustained focus on the influence of anthropogenic forces over climate systems has helped put their regional impacts into focus. AchutaRao has been associated with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change since 2001, rising to become a contributing author to the seminal reports in its fifth and sixth editions. He also helped set up IIT’s Centre of Excellence for Climate Change Adaptation, which developed an expertise in climate risk assessments and adaptation planning for heat extremes, monsoon variability, and other hazards affecting vulnerable communities in India. But apart from his scientific contributions, AchutaRao was also an advocate of raising awareness about climate change. He engaged with the media often to explain the importance of limiting global heating, and spoke of how its uneven impacts on the developing world could affect people, institutions, and countries. “This is a very critical time in our history, because we are a developing country poised to take off. Most of our development is yet to happen, in spite of what you might see,” he said in an interview to an IIT student in 2020. “So in that development, how are we going to make sure we don’t make the same high emission mistakes the rest of the developed world has made? item.content:encoded: Nepal’s long-held policy of harnessing hydroelectricity and using it for economic growth has met new challenges: potential catastrophic floods in the snow-fed rivers amid rising global temperatures. The August 26 floods that originated on the Nepal-China border, and that knocked out around 10% of installed power from the national grid, has prompted a debate on whether Nepal should rethink its overall hydropower strategy or just adopt better-engineered plants. Amid this, the flood could jeopardise the country’s clean energy targets and push it to adopt more solar power. Immediate impacts The recent flash flood crippled a combined installed generation capacity of 281 megawatts, including a solar power plant, and damaged four other under-construction projects, totaling a capacity of 700 MW. One of the oldest hydroelectric plants, the 14.1-MW Devighat Hydroelectric Plant, commissioned 42 years ago, was wiped out. Further downstream, the flood badly damaged a 25-MW solar power plant, according to data compiled by Mongabay from official sources. Similarly, with a hub of a transmission line washed away on the Trishuli river’s banks, another 150 MW of power from different power plants is cut off from the national grid system. Transmission lines, including a substation on the Trishuli riverbank, were also destroyed. While officials are assessing the damage, estimates put losses at hundreds of billions of Nepali rupees, according to media reports. They say they can’t yet provide timelines for when the affected projects will resume generation. item.content:encoded: This is Part 1 of a series on exotic pet trade. The series looks at the health impacts, legal challenges and the ecological consequences of keeping exotic wild animals as pets. Mumbai-based veterinarian Dr. Rina Dev was hospitalised for four days recently with a lung infection. “I hope it’s not something from the parrots I was treating,” she told Mongabay-India after being discharged from the hospital. Dr. Dev is an avian and exotic animal veterinarian who works closely with the forest department to treat imported and seized exotic animals involved in the wildlife trade. Her concerns are valid. Avian chlamydiosis, or psittacosis, is caused by the bacterium Chlamydia psittaci and is a common infection among people who handle birds, earning it the nickname “bird handler’s disease”. A 2024 case from India describes a man contracting the infection after exposure to his pet parrot. In 1994, customs officers in Belgium contracted chlamydiosis after being exposed to infected parakeets. Multiple such documented cases link wildlife trade to human infection. A comprehensive review of psittacosis by the ICAR-Indian Veterinary Research Institute in 2021 describes avian chlamydiosis as a “neglected disease” with “critical zoonotic potential”. Pet trade link to zoonosis Zoonoses, or zoonotic diseases, entered the ordinary Indian’s wellness lexicon when the COVID-19 pandemic exposed how pathogens can jump from animals to humans, causing serious medical consequences and, in some cases, a pandemic that can literally bring the world to a standstill.
